title: He emptied himself (Philippians 2:5–11)
hookLine: the early hymn of Christ taking the form of a servant

lines: A HYMN TO CHRIST BEFORE DAWN.
cards: Around the year 112, a Roman governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan about the Christians in his province. He'd questioned some of them.
They met on a fixed day before dawn, he reported, and sang a hymn to Christ as to a god. We don't have their words.
But many scholars think one of the earliest Christian hymns sits in today's passage, older than the letter it's in, quoted by Paul to his friends in Philippi.

teach.h: LET THIS MIND BE IN YOU.
teach.b: Paul sets it up with a request: in humility, count others better than yourselves. "For let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus."

Then the hymn: "Who being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and in habit found as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even to the death of the cross."
Emptied himself. The Greek verb is ekenōsen, and from it comes today's word: kenosis, self-emptying. Emptied of what?
Paul doesn't spell it out. Catholic teaching, following the Council of Chalcedon, holds that he did not stop being God.

teach.h: STILL GOD, TAKING A SERVANT'S FORM.
teach.b: He emptied himself by taking on what he was not: a human nature, a servant's form, a death reserved for slaves and rebels. The hymn goes down: God, servant, man, death, the cross.
Then it turns and goes up: God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth."

teach.h: DOWN TO THE CROSS, THEN RAISED UP.
teach.b: Down to the lowest point, then raised to the highest. Paul isn't writing a doctrine lesson. He's asking a quarrelsome church to have the same mind: go down first.
Catholics hear this hymn every year on Palm Sunday, at the start of Holy Week. And at Mass, the liturgy's instructions still call for a bow of the head at the name of Jesus.

how: Catholics hear the hymn of Philippians 2 as the second reading on Palm Sunday, and the liturgy calls for a bow of the head at the name of Jesus.

games.q: you are in the form of God, equal with God. what do you do with it?
o: hold onto it as something to be grasped.
empty yourself, taking the form of a servant.
use it to rule the world from above.
games.why: "he thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant."

practice: Think of one thing you hold onto that keeps you above other people: the need to be right, to get credit, to be served first.
Picture taking it out of your pocket and setting it on the table, and notice how it feels to be without it, even for a minute.
If you pray, say the name of Jesus slowly and bow your head; if not, simply bow your head, and let it stay on the table.

wordCard.voice: Kenosis. Greek for self-emptying, from Philippians: Christ, in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: emptying, from the verb ekenōsen, 'he emptied' (Philippians 2:7).

carryVoice: Your line: obedient unto death. Down to the lowest point, then raised up. See you tomorrow.
